candidateRows: Treating naturalism as a positive denial of anything supernatural improperly shifts the burden of proof onto nonbelievers.
This establishes the con side's governing interpretation of the motion and its central burden-of-proof objection.
Aron Ra opens by disputing the framing of naturalism as a truth-valued positive doctrine and compares that framing with burden shifting over atheism.
Acceptance of the physical world does not itself establish the stronger claim that no immaterial or supernatural reality exists.
The distinction limits what the con side must defend and challenges an asserted equivalence among naturalism, physicalism, and materialism.
The speaker distinguishes ordinary realism about a material world from a positive exclusion of all supernatural alternatives and notes definitional ambiguity.
Methodological naturalism is justified because scientific claims must rest on testable evidence, while supernatural claims have produced no reliable demonstrations.
This supplies the con side's affirmative evidential rationale for naturalistic scientific practice and its rejection of supernatural explanations.
Aron Ra defines methodological naturalism through evidence, testing, and falsifiability, then argues that purported supernatural practitioners have shown no dependable success.
Anyone seeking to refute naturalism must substantiate a supernatural alternative rather than require naturalists to prove an undefined negative.
The move states the con side's proposed burden allocation and its direct standard for resolving the debate motion.
Aron Ra offers to consider legitimate evidence for supernatural reality but refuses to prove that no undefined immaterial alternative exists.
Metaphysical naturalism claims that only the natural world is real and therefore carries a burden of proof in a debate over whether it is true.
This defines the proposition the pro side contests and directly rejects the con side's proposed refusal of a burden of proof.
Aron Ra's claim that he need not prove an undefined supernatural negative and may place the burden entirely on Wood
David Wood distinguishes metaphysical naturalism from methodological naturalism and argues that affirming the former in this debate requires supporting it.
A method that automatically reinterprets every possible contrary observation can reject any position and is therefore not a rational evidential methodology.
The argument challenges the skeptical evidential posture Wood associates with the con side and prepares his critique of naturalism's epistemic foundations.
Aron Ra's evidence-centered demand that Wood substantiate supernatural reality while Aron declines a positive defense of naturalism
Wood uses analogies involving flat-earth denial and proving another person's existence to argue that unrestricted skeptical reinterpretation defeats any evidence.
Naturalism is catastrophically self-undermining because accepting its account of cognition removes rational warrant for trusting the cognition that affirms it.
This is the pro side's principal thesis and directly states the evolutionary-naturalist cognitive-reliability critique posed by the motion.
After illustrating self-undermining hypotheses with an omnipotent deceiver, Wood argues that naturalistically produced faculties were not made for judging naturalism.
If beliefs result entirely from nonrational physical causes governed by natural laws rather than truth, naturalism supplies no basis for trusting those beliefs.
This provides the causal mechanism for the central self-undermining argument by separating belief production from sensitivity to truth.
Wood characterizes cognition under naturalism as physical cause and effect, arguing that the same indifferent processes determine both true and false beliefs.
Natural selection favors survival and reproduction rather than truth, so evolved faculties lack warrant when extended to abstract claims such as naturalism.
The move supplies the evolutionary component of the pro case and answers the anticipated claim that selection generally produces reliable cognition.
Wood argues that false beliefs can aid fitness, that selection rewards practical behavior, and that faculties shaped for basic tasks are unreliable in metaphysics.
Human social evolution favored empathy, cooperation, trustworthiness, and widening concern, giving selection reasons to preserve dependable social cognition.
This is the con side's first direct evolutionary answer to the claim that selection rewards only selfish fitness rather than dependable cognition and conduct.
David Wood's argument that natural selection targets mere survival and reproduction without favoring reliable truth-directed cognitive faculties
Aron Ra argues that humans survived through group solidarity and empathy, while persistently selfish or unreliable individuals were socially excluded across generations.
Naturalists need not prove a negative when supernaturalists have not supplied evidence for any supernatural aspect of reality.
This directly contests where the burden lies in a debate over naturalism and challenges the claim that withholding supernatural belief is irrational.
Wood's demand that the naturalist defend naturalism and his characterization of naturalistic confidence as irrational.
After completing an evolutionary account of social morality, Aron turns to Wood's supernatural skepticism standard, burden allocation, and cognitive-reliability criticism.
An affirmative atheist position can be defended because there is evidence against souls and major scriptural supernatural claims, not merely an absence of supporting evidence.
The move answers the demand for an affirmative case and supplies a claimed evidential basis for rejecting central supernatural propositions.
Wood's contention that Aron avoids defending an affirmative worldview while placing the entire burden on supernaturalists.
Following examples of belief-shaped religious experiences, Aron distinguishes lack-of-belief atheism from his stronger position and claims counterevidence to supernatural doctrines.
If naturalism makes every assertion the causally determined product of particles in motion, naturalists lack a rational basis for taking either participant's assertions seriously.
This states the core cognitive-reliability critique by arguing that a naturalistic causal origin of belief undercuts rational confidence in the resulting worldview.
Aron's preceding evidential and experiential defense of naturalism and his claim to reason rationally from the available evidence.
David begins his response by reframing everything Aron said as naturalistically determined physical output, then invokes Darwin's doubt about higher convictions.
Evolutionary explanations for empathy and cooperative herd behavior do not establish reliable cognitive faculties for discovering comprehensive truths about the universe.
The reply separates the adaptive value of social behavior from truth-tracking on grand worldview questions, preserving the critique against Aron's evolutionary explanation.
Aron's account of empathy, cooperation, ostracism, and morality as products of evolutionary population mechanics.
David grants that concern for fellow group members can aid survival but denies that this provides grounds for trusting cognition about naturalism or cosmic truth.
Evolutionary naturalism generates several defeaters for worldview belief, including causal determinism, epiphenomenal mental states, and selection for survival rather than cosmic truth.
This is the most developed statement of the affirmative case, specifying multiple mechanisms by which naturalism allegedly undermines confidence in naturalistic conclusions.
Aron's claim that Wood mistakenly attributes cognitive self-undermining to evolution and fails to understand evolutionary mechanics.
David distinguishes evolution alone from evolution combined with naturalism, then explains determinism, Huxley's train-whistle analogy, and survival-selected faculties.

A naturalism that can reinterpret every conceivable apparent manifestation of God as aliens or another natural cause becomes insulated from contrary evidence and is not a good-faith evidential position.
The move challenges the falsifiability and evidential openness of the opposing worldview, supporting the claim that demands for supernatural evidence may be impossible to satisfy.
Aron's claim that empirical propositions can be proved to sincere interlocutors and that good-faith evidential engagement is the key distinction.
David agrees that good- and bad-faith discussions differ, then argues that prominent naturalists precommit to natural reinterpretations of any apparent divine evidence.
Because both sides accept the known natural world, the person adding a supernatural realm bears the burden of justifying that addition through independent, repeatable, objective verification.
This supplies the con side's central burden-of-proof framework and states the empirical conditions under which a supernatural addition could become justified.
Wood's argument that naturalism itself requires defense and that naturalists are committed to rejecting any possible supernatural evidence.
Aron rejects the proposed burden shift, says Wood offered no supernatural evidence, and describes regular, independent, testable confirmation as the appropriate standard.

Metaphysical naturalism resembles solipsism because it can reinterpret every possible challenge within its own framework, yet its adherents still avoid defending their comprehensive position while trusting unreliable cognition.
The analogy unifies the affirmative challenges concerning burden of proof, insulation from rebuttal, and confidence in faculties whose reliability naturalism allegedly compromises.
Aron's refusal to accept the burden for naturalism and his appeal to personal investigation as support for rejecting supernatural claims.
David compares naturalism with an unfalsifiable solipsistic worldview, argues that holding a comprehensive metaphysics carries a burden, and closes with the charge of faith.

Aron's personal skeptical experience cannot justify dismissing vast numbers of reported miracles, especially if naturalism already gives him reason to doubt the reliability of his own cognitive faculties.
This applies the affirmative reliability critique to Aron's evidential judgments and challenges the scope of the inference from his personal debunking experiences to others' reports.
Aron's distinction between deceptive subjective experience and failed objective verification of his former supernatural beliefs.
David argues that others report contrary experiences, extrapolates from a survey of miracle reports, and says Aron claims excessive certainty despite naturalistic cognitive limits.
Repeated objective failure of supernatural claims, together with explicit conditions that would change his mind, supports naturalism without claiming omniscience or insulating it from evidence.
The move directly answers the alleged self-defeat and unfalsifiability of naturalism by grounding confidence in repeated testing and specifying potentially disconfirming evidence.
Wood's charge that Aron dismisses widespread miracle testimony through an unreliable naturalistic faculty amounting to near-omniscience.
Aron denies making the attributed claim, cites the collapse of previously accepted paranormal evidence, accepts a burden to state standards, and asks Wood for positive verification.
Naturalism should be evaluated objectively, and rejecting it requires demonstrating some supernatural addition rather than merely criticizing a participant's beliefs.
The move states Aron's central burden-of-proof account for the motion and challenges Wood to identify an objectively demonstrable supernatural alternative.
Wood's earlier cognitive-reliability critique and characterization of Aron's naturalist position.
After disputing Wood's description of his beliefs, Aron distinguishes the debate's objective question from his personal history and demands evidence of anything beyond nature.
A defender cannot establish a worldview merely by demanding that opponents disprove it, as illustrated by an analogous defense of metaphysical solipsism.
The analogy directly contests Aron's allocation of the burden of proof and supports Wood's claim that naturalism itself requires a positive rational defense.
Aron's claim that Wood must disprove naturalism by showing that something supernatural exists.
Wood compares Aron's defense of naturalism with a solipsist who treats the failure to prove an external world as sufficient support for solipsism.
Whether framed as asserting only nature or merely acknowledging the known natural world, Wood still bears the burden of showing that something beyond nature exists.
This is Aron's principal procedural and substantive answer: naturalism remains warranted absent a demonstrated supernatural exception to the observed natural world.
Wood's metaphysical-solipsism analogy and claim that naturalism needs its own positive case.
Aron dismisses the analogy as a different debate, accepts the stated naturalist position for purposes of this debate, and reiterates Wood's evidential burden.
Naturalism can be rejected without proving supernaturalism because its account of nonrational causes and survival-oriented cognition makes confident affirmation of the worldview incoherent.
The move presents the debate's core cognitive-reliability critique and explains why internal incoherence alone could defeat rational confidence in naturalism.
Aron's contention that the only relevant route to rejecting naturalism is demonstrating a supernatural reality.
Wood argues that a worldview may be defeated internally, then claims naturalism gives cognition only nonrational, survival-directed origins unsuited to judging all reality.
Humans must provisionally accept sensory experience as reality, and Wood's skepticism does not relieve him of showing an exception to the natural world.
The move answers the global skepticism argument while preserving Aron's core contention that Wood must supply evidence for something beyond the natural world.
Wood's claim that naturalism undermines trust in faculties used to affirm naturalism or assess reality.
Aron answers that ordinary reliance on perception is unavoidable and argues that under either naturalist formulation Wood still must demonstrate something else exists.
Humean and Darwinian doubts about the reach of human cognition show that one can withhold affirmation of naturalism without affirming any supernatural alternative.
The move supplies historical examples for Wood's central distinction between withholding rational confidence in naturalism and positively defending supernaturalism.
Aron's insistence that rejecting naturalism requires evidence for a supernatural alternative.
Wood argues that Hume and Darwin would question their competence to judge ultimate reality, making agnosticism about naturalism a coherent outcome without supernatural commitment.
Objective data rather than authorities or personal experiences should govern belief, and Wood has not supplied objective verification of anything supernatural.
The move condenses Aron's epistemic standard and directly contrasts publicly verifiable data with both testimonial experience and Wood's cognitive skepticism.
Wood's appeal to Darwin, Hume, Dawkins, and doubts about naturalistically produced cognitive faculties.
Aron denies treating Dawkins as an authority, says personal experiences proved unreliable, and maintains that Wood has not met the requested objective evidential standard.

If beliefs result from causally determined particles, epiphenomenal mental states, and faculties selected only for survival, naturalists lack grounds for trusting those faculties about ultimate reality.
This closing synthesis states the pro side's complete cognitive-reliability case and applies it directly to the rational affirmation of naturalism.
Aron's reliance on objective data and his denial that natural origins make human reasoning irrational.
Wood argues that deterministic physical causes, causally idle mental states, and survival-selected faculties cannot justify sweeping judgments about reality or naturalism itself.
Emergent bottom-up processes explain apparent design, while supernatural and religious claims remain unverified or falsified and must establish possibility before probability or fact.
The closing integrates Aron's naturalistic explanation of apparent design with his evidential case that supernatural alternatives have not cleared even the threshold of possibility.
Wood's closing claim that naturalistic emergence and evolved cognition cannot support rational confidence.
Aron rejects Wood's characterization, presents design as an emergent bottom-up appearance, and argues that religious, miraculous, and other supernatural claims consistently lack verification.
A supernatural event would leave natural effects that remain open to natural reinterpretation, so identifying it depends on evidential patterns rather than a simple measuring device.
The answer addresses the central verification challenge by explaining why supernatural causation may not be directly measurable even when its resulting physical effects are observable.
The audience question asking for a consistent method of measuring a supernatural or non-natural world.
Wood concedes that he lacks a consistent supernatural measurement procedure, then argues that miraculous effects become ordinary physical facts susceptible to alternative natural explanations.
If purported magic or miracles consistently produced observable effects that defied physical explanation, they would constitute discoverable evidence of the supernatural.
The move supplies the naturalist side's evidential criterion for supernatural claims and explains why the absence of reproducible examples matters.
David Wood's claim that supernatural occurrences would become naturally describable immediately after occurring.
After Wood says supernatural intervention could always be redescribed naturally, Aron distinguishes lawful observable magic from unsupported claims and reports finding no evidence for it.
Religious prophecies commonly reflect retrospective revision, and the few verifiably prior predictions can fail rather than establish supernatural knowledge.
This move directly contests prophecy as independent evidence for supernaturalism by offering a general alternative explanation and a claimed counterexample.
The audience claim that Zoroastrian and biblical predictions were fulfilled and therefore indicate supernatural involvement.
An audience member cites pre-Christian and biblical predictions; Aron cautions that popular prophecy parallels often cannot be verified and argues that retrospective fitting is widespread.
Belief in supernatural reality does not require accepting every miracle report, because individual reports can range from weak or naturalistically explicable to genuinely suggestive.
The move protects the cognitive-reliability critique from depending on indiscriminate credulity and articulates a discriminating approach to miracle testimony.
The prophecy discussion and the broader skeptical suggestion that failed or dubious religious claims discredit supernatural belief.
Following Aron's criticism of prophecy claims, Wood separates general supernatural belief from acceptance of particular reports and describes assessing cases according to their evidential strength.
Naturalism supplies cognitive faculties shaped for survival while treating them as reliable for conclusions far beyond verification, creating tension within the worldview itself.
This is a compact restatement of the debate's central pro contention that evolutionary naturalism undermines confidence in the reasoning used to affirm naturalism.
The questioner's claim that collaborative confirmation handles cognitive limitations and challenge to treating rationality as supernatural.

A naturalist questioner points to measurable cognitive error and collaborative checking; Wood replies that the problem concerns confidence beyond verification given naturalism's own account of cognition.
A documented apparent healing should be considered rather than dismissed, but prior experience with misrepresented supporting literature justifies initial doubt pending examination.
The response defines the con side's stated openness to contrary evidence while explaining why extraordinary testimonial claims do not presently overturn naturalism.
The audience member's medically documented vocal-cord recovery offered as a potentially compelling miracle case.
Asked whether a recorded and medically documented recovery would make miracles possible, Aron says he would examine the documentation while retaining doubts based on repeated citation failures.
Rejecting naturalism for self-undermining incoherence does not establish supernaturalism; it can instead warrant withholding affirmation of either worldview.
The move clarifies the pro side's burden and central conclusion: the argument seeks suspension of confidence in naturalism rather than direct proof of the supernatural.
The audience questioner's characterization of David as asserting that reality contains more than the natural world.
When an audience member treats Wood as asserting supernatural reality, Wood separates his personal beliefs from the debate argument and says naturalism may be rejected without affirming its opposite.
Naturalistic cognition is either causally determined or affected by randomness, neither of which adds rational control, whereas theism can ground cognition in a truth-directed purpose.
This move defends the proposed link between naturalism and unreliable cognition while presenting the theistic account as capable of supplying a truth-oriented source.
The audience objection that determinism need not follow from naturalism and would be experientially indistinguishable from free will.
After a challenge to the determinism premise, Wood argues that quantum randomness would not improve reasoning and contrasts survival-shaped faculties with cognition created for understanding truth.
A deliberately rational machine could be trusted because of its programming, but evolved humans are selected for survival and reproduction rather than reliable grand metaphysical theorizing.
The machine analogy sharpens the principal pro argument by locating the reliability deficit not in determinism alone but in the evolutionary purpose assigned to cognition.
The audience challenge that a fully deterministic machine programmed to reason rationally could still be considered reliable.

Asked why determinism would make a rational machine unreliable, Wood grants reliability under rational programming but denies that naturalism gives human cognition an analogous truth-directed function.
Wood's descriptions of determinism and rationality do not match the naturalist account being defended, so the alleged incompatibility between naturalism and rational thought is unsupported.
The move attacks a key premise of the cognitive-reliability critique by disputing the conceptual account used to connect naturalism, determinism, and irrationality.
David Wood's argument that survival-oriented deterministic cognition cannot reliably support a comprehensive theory such as naturalism.
Aron acknowledges limited formal philosophy study but maintains that neither reality nor rationality fits Wood's descriptions and that the claimed failure of naturalist rationality does not follow.
If a naturalist account permits a genuine alternative to determinism, the determinism premise can be dropped without exhausting the remaining arguments against confidence in naturalism.
The concession narrows the scope of the pro case and makes explicit that its broader cognitive-reliability critique is intended to survive loss of the determinism premise.
Aron Ra's objection that determinism is not an accurate or necessary description of naturalistic reality and rationality.
Following Aron's conceptual objection, Wood says he is unaware of a naturalist alternative beyond indeterministic quantum events but would abandon the determinism point if such a view exists.
